newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. suggests easing sanctions on Burundi.
newsitem.headline: U.S. suggests easing sanctions on Burundi.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher has urged East African leaders to consider easing sanctions on Burundi, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
During talks in Arusha before flying to Cape Town, he told the leaders they should recognise progress toward national reconciliation made by Burundi's military rulers.

Christopher stopped short of explicitly saying sanctions adjustments should take place now because that decision must be taken by the regional leaders, who hold a summit on Burundi in Arusha on Saturday, officials told reporters aboard Christopher's airplane.

But Christopher "discussed with virtually everyone of our interlocutors ... that if the parties respond positively to the urgings and desires of the international community -- that is to do things that would favour the prospects of negotiations and a negotiated settlement -- that there needs to be some acknowledgment of that progress," one senior official said.

The secretary also made clear the U.S. view that Burundi military leader Major Pierre Buyoya in recent days "has taken some positive steps" toward national reconciliation by reinstituting parliament and unbanning political parties, officials said. He also stressed that more needs to be done.
"The secretary in his discussions said, and others agreed, that there should be some effort to acknowledge progress when and as it is made," one official said.

On the third leg of a five-nation African tour, Christopher met in Arusha with Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa, Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and former Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere, the international mediator on Burundi.

He later flew to Cape Town for talks on Saturday with South African President Nelson Mandela, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who heads the post-apartheid era Truth and Renconciliation Commission.
At a news conference and in a written statement before leaving Arusha, Christopher alluded to the message officials say he passed on to regional leaders.
"When we see progress we must be willing to recognise it," Christopher said.
"Both sides have expressed a willingness to negotiate. Mr Buyoya's decision to reopen the National Assembly and to lift the ban on political parties is encouraging," he added.

East African leaders will decide whether to ease, tighten, or lift an economic and transport embargo on Burundi since Buyoya, a Tutsi army officer and former president, ousted civilian Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya in coup last July.

Diplomats said the United States believed Buyoya should come in person to Arusha to present his case to the presidents of Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Zambia, the premier of Zaire and officials of the Organisation of African Unity.
But Buyoya says he must be invited as the head of state.

One official said even if summit leaders ease sanctions "there is an understanding that some sanctions are going to have to remain in place pretty much throughout this process of negotiations ... until there is some agreement ...and significant progress toward implementation of that agreement."
